html:
The migration of Chinese men to California after gold was found there in 1848. Most came from a few counties in the Pearl River Delta of Guangdong, sailing from Hong Kong to San Francisco. They called California Gold Mountain.

Push and pull worked together. At home the Opium War, poverty and later the Taiping Rebellion made life hard; in America the California Gold Rush promised quick money. By the early 1850s tens of thousands had arrived. White miners resented them, and California taxed foreign miners and pushed the Chinese onto worked-out claims.

From 1865 the Central Pacific Railroad hired Chinese workers in large numbers, and they made up most of its labour force. They blasted tunnels through the Sierra Nevada, and many died in accidents and avalanches, to finish the first transcontinental railroad in 1869.

Hostility grew as the economy slowed. In 1882 Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, the first American law to bar a people by nationality. Chinese miners also went to the gold fields of Victoria in Australia.
